paragraphs.heading: Two centuries of Roman Peace
paragraphs.text: The Pax Romana, Latin for "Roman Peace", was a stretch of roughly 200 years seen as a golden age for ancient Rome: stable, prosperous, dominant and growing, with relative peace and order. It is usually dated from 27 BC, when Augustus rose to power and founded the principate, to AD 180, when Marcus Aurelius, the last of the "Five Good Emperors", died. It counts among the longest-lasting periods of peace in history. It was not free of fighting, though; there were still revolts inside the empire and wars outside it, including the Roman–Persian wars.

paragraphs.heading: Size, people and trade
paragraphs.text: In these years the empire reached its greatest extent, under Trajan in 117. Its population is thought to have reached a peak of 70 million people, about 33% of everyone in the world. Trade across the Mediterranean grew, bringing big profits and higher incomes, and Romans sailed east for silks, gems, onyx and spices. At about the same time Han China held its own Pax Sinica in the East, and together the two eras gave a strong push to long-distance travel and trade across Eurasia.

paragraphs.heading: How Augustus made peace
paragraphs.text: For most historians the Pax Romana began when Octavian, later Augustus, beat Mark Antony and Cleopatra at the Battle of Actium on 2 September 31 BC. With no good example of one-man rule to follow, he bound Rome's greatest military leaders into a ruling group and acted as its front man, which removed the risk of civil war. Peace did not come at once, since fighting went on in Hispania and the Alps. Still, he closed the Gates of Janus, a ceremony showing that Rome was at peace, in 29 BC and 25 BC, and a third time that scholars date to 13 BC.

paragraphs.heading: Selling the idea of peace
paragraphs.text: Romans did not see peace as just the absence of war. To them it was a rare state that came only once every enemy had been beaten down and could no longer resist. Augustus had to persuade them that the wealth of peacetime was worth more to the empire than the riches and honor a risky war might win, and he managed it with skillful propaganda. Later emperors followed him with lavish ceremonies at the Gates of Janus, coins bearing Pax, and literature praising the peace. The earliest known use of the term Pax Romana is in a text by Seneca the Younger from AD 55.

paragraphs.heading: Law across the empire
paragraphs.text: Legal ideas spread in this period too. The Jus Gentium, a set of basic rights, began in the empire, and principles still used today, such as "innocent until proven guilty", reached towns, villages and hamlets. People became more aware of the rights of citizens. Circuit courts met on a fixed schedule, so citizens had less need to take the law into their own hands.

paragraphs.heading: A peace worth questioning
paragraphs.text: Historians debate the label. Walter Goffart noted that the volume of the Cambridge Ancient History covering AD 70–192 is titled "The Imperial Peace", yet peace is not what its pages describe. Madden puts the true start in the 2nd century BC, once Rome had removed all its serious military rivals. Tim Cornell also dates a peace without major wars between states to that century. Arnaldo Momigliano called the Pax Romana an easy formula for propaganda but a hard subject to study.
